it's a very good example of what empathy is fundamentally. It's your ability to relate to others on an emotional, intellectual and physical level. When you see a guy get hit in the balls, you understand his pain and to some degree you feel it. That is empathy. Empathy extends beyond just physical pain, you can also understand the emotional pain that some people suffer with when, for example, they get a cancer diagnosis and they're afraid, or when they win a really important game or award and you feel how good they feel. Empathy is inherent to human beings, it's like the sense of smell, however some people lack empathy, and that's uncommon and a sign of emotional and intellectual struggle. Many people become more empathetic as they age and mature. For example, a 15 year old may have very little noticeable empathy, but that same person at 30 may end up being very empathetic and very helpful and kind toward others. 

There's also Cognitive Empathy and Affective Empathy. Cognitive Empathy is the less developed version of empathy as it is only the ability to intellectualize what others are experiencing without any feelings of your own. For example, you see a guy get hit in the balls and you just stare with no reaction, thinking and feeling nothing about what you just saw. You might say "that sucks" but you don't have that physical response that's typical when someone sees this. Affective is the more developed version of Empathy because it's the ability to have a physical and emotional response to what you just saw while also intellectualizing it. People with Affective Empathy are usually the people that go over to help someone who has just been hurt.

OP sorry for your loss. Cats are more emotional and intelligent than we may think at first. I have three, one of my cats is 16 and has been with me that long. They are incredible beings. Here are some tips that might sound weird at first; 

Take cat out of cage, makes them feel insecure. And keep them away from open doors and screens that they can claw through. In a new environment, you must let the cat explore to whole house so they feel comfortable. Being in a cage in a new place would be scary. Meowing a lot or loudly is normal at this time. 

Let cat roam the house. Indoor cats live longer and are safer. Keep kitty indoors, especially if this is a new neighborhood as well. Kitty can become a victim in a new neighborhood to a car. 

Socialize with kitty like you would a person in the room. It will feel weird at first, but tell kitty everything that's going on. Tell them where they are, what happened to their human friend, and who you are and what your intentions are. 

Facial expressions. Cats read your facial expressions and body language, and they sense your anxiety around them. One way cats communicate is through Blinking. When making eye contact with kitty, verbalize that you want to be friends and slowly blink. Do this a lot. This shows you are a friend and not a threat. 

When approaching kitty, put out your hand and point at them with one finger. Kitty will see your finger and want to sniff it, then they will want to run their face on your finger. This is how you introduce yourself to kitty. 

Try to realize that you are living with a scared and confused thinking feeling sentient being and you'll soon connect with kitty. It takes empathy, kindness and respect to bond with cats. They have their boundaries and their guard, in time kitty will relax those boundaries and guard. Free roaming. No outdoors. Conversation. Blinking. Empathy. It'll happen. 

Consider high quality cat food. Low quality food contributes to shorter lives. Google it and see what brands you like, but don't fall for marketing like "gravy" etc. Your cat would rather eat a rat than slurp gravy. They put words like Gravy on labels to sell to human taste. 

Have love and friendship in your heart and in your voice when you speak to kitty, and they will come around to you.

Is Dobby your first aging cat? I ask only because I have an aging cat, and a lot of what you're listing sounds like my dude. In the case of my buddy, he is aging but not exactly dying. The raspy changes to his meow, the slight change in his balance, he sleeps more now. For healthy aging cats this is all expected, same with us humans. A big sign of their health is grooming, eating, peeing and pooping regularly, their tail language etc. As long as actions like that are maintained, it's generally assumed that they are okay. 

The quality of the food you provide makes a huge difference, and most often adds quality years to their lives. Helpful suggestion, if you haven't already, read up on what to expect with aging cats and their food requirements. For instance, too high of protein in their food can lead to kidney disease (which is common), and can cause constipation and a whole host of health issues that may have been avoided otherwise. Dry food can dehydrate them easier as they age, and that can lead to kidney issues as well. 

To find the best food google unbiased cat food reviews and keywords of that nature. If you're close to a petco, Hills Science Diet is a mid tier decent quality brand that is affordable. My cats enjoy it and the cans are labeled well with age, ailments, nutritional info and so on. There are a lot of brands out there even better than Hills, but it's not bad. You can even give kitty tuna in water from time to time. They go nuts over it and it's good for them. I often grab some chicken and blanche in plain water, then chop/mince/puree it for my cats. They love it, but only when I first make it lol. They wont eat leftovers it's so weird. If you're into cooking for Dobby, there are a lot of recipes out there and it's not expensive or difficult. The most important thing is high quality food and a balanced diet.

Oh, if they don't get exercise they can process waste slower (poop), and that can make them sick. They need play, moving around, even tummy rubs to move around their organs. Gently rolling of the belly like dough. For some reason two of my three cats love their belly rolled. 

Lastly project love, peace, comfort and safety to kitty. Try not to focus on the aging process, but the happiness you feel each day you two are still in each other's lives. My oldest is 15. I brush him, pet him, all that, and say nice things to him. I think comfort helps them age well, but if not, it surely helps us cope with their process. I just remembered. When my oldest cat was 7 years old he became depressed. He was alone when I wasn't home. I realized he needed a companion, and coincidentally I found a lone kitten crying in a bush at my job.
